questions.stem: A home appraised at $410,000 sold two weeks later for $425,000 after a bidding war. The $425,000 figure is best described as the property's
questions.explanation: Market price is what a buyer actually paid. Market value is the appraiser's estimate of the most probable price under typical conditions ($410,000 here); the two can differ when buyers compete or are under pressure.

questions.stem: An appraiser concludes a vacant lot's most valuable use would be a 12-story office building, but zoning allows only three stories. Which highest and best use test does the 12-story building fail?
questions.explanation: Highest and best use must be legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive. A use the zoning doesn't allow fails the legally permissible test, no matter how profitable it would be.

questions.stem: An owner spent $45,000 on an in-ground pool. An appraiser finds the pool adds $15,000 to the home's value. Under the principle of contribution, what is the pool worth?
questions.explanation: Contribution says a component is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. The pool contributes $15,000; the other $30,000 of its cost is not recovered in value.

questions.stem: A builder in a subdivision of similar two-story traditional homes proposes an ultramodern design that looks nothing like its neighbors. Which principle suggests the unusual design may hurt its value?
questions.explanation: Conformity holds that value is maximized when a property is reasonably similar to its neighbors in style, age and use. A home that departs sharply from the neighborhood tends to lose value.

questions.stem: Which principle of value holds that value is the present worth of expected future benefits, and is the basis of the income approach?
questions.explanation: Anticipation looks forward: a buyer pays today for the benefits (such as income) the property is expected to produce. That is why it drives the income approach. Substitution compares the cost of an equally desirable alternative.

questions.stem: For a single-family home in an active market, an appraiser's three approaches indicate $395,000 (sales comparison), $420,000 (cost) and $380,000 (income). How does the appraiser reach a final opinion of value?
choices: Averages the three to get about $398,333
Reconciles them, weighting sales comparison most
Uses the $420,000 cost figure because it is the highest
Uses the income figure because it is the most conservative
questions.explanation: Reconciliation weights the approach best suited to the property type; it is not a simple average. For a single-family home with many recent sales, sales comparison gets the most weight.

questions.stem: A 2,400 sq ft building would cost $175 per sq ft to replace. Accrued depreciation is $84,000 and the land is worth $110,000. What is the value indicated by the cost approach?
questions.explanation: Cost new: 2,400 × $175 = $420,000. Less depreciation: $420,000 − $84,000 = $336,000. Add land: $336,000 + $110,000 = $446,000. Forgetting the land gives $336,000; skipping depreciation gives $530,000.

questions.stem: An appraiser valuing a 1920s home estimates the cost to build a structure with the same usefulness using modern materials and methods. This estimate is the
questions.explanation: Replacement cost is a building of equal utility built with modern materials, and it is the more common choice. Reproduction cost is an exact replica using the same materials and methods.

questions.stem: A small apartment building has potential gross income of $120,000, vacancy and collection loss of 6%, and operating expenses of $46,800. The owner's annual mortgage payments are $30,000. Using an 8% capitalization rate, what is its value?
questions.explanation: EGI = $120,000 − 6% ($7,200) = $112,800. NOI = $112,800 − $46,800 = $66,000. Value = $66,000 ÷ 0.08 = $825,000. Mortgage payments are debt service, not an operating expense, so subtracting them (giving $450,000) is wrong.

questions.stem: An online home value estimate is produced by software from public-record and recent sales data, without anyone inspecting the home. What is it?
questions.explanation: An automated valuation model (AVM) estimates value from data alone. Because it can't see condition, upgrades or view, it is least reliable where there are few similar sales. A BPO or CMA is prepared by a broker, and an appraisal by a credentialed appraiser.

questions.stem: In a lien-theory state, who holds legal title to a financed home while the loan is being repaid?
choices: A trustee chosen by the lender
questions.explanation: Under lien theory, the borrower keeps title and the lender holds only a lien. Under title theory, legal title goes to the lender or a trustee until the loan is paid, while the borrower keeps equitable title and possession.

questions.stem: A seller sells a lot and carries back a loan secured by it. The buyer needs a construction loan, and the construction lender insists on first lien position. Which clause in the seller's loan makes this possible?
questions.explanation: In a subordination clause the lender agrees its lien will rank behind a later lien, which is common when a land loan will be followed by a construction loan. Acceleration, defeasance and alienation clauses deal with default, payoff and transfer.

questions.stem: A developer's blanket loan covers 20 lots. Which clause lets a single lot be freed from the lien when it sells and the developer pays down a set amount?
questions.explanation: A release clause lets individual parcels come out from under a blanket loan as they are sold. The defeasance clause is different: it requires the lender to release the whole lien once the entire debt is paid.

questions.stem: A borrower wants to pay off her loan two years early by refinancing. Her lender says she owes an extra fee for doing so. Which clause allows this charge?
questions.explanation: A prepayment penalty clause charges a fee for paying off early. Without one, a borrower may generally prepay. The alienation clause is triggered by a transfer of the property, not by early payoff.

questions.stem: A lender collects one-twelfth of the annual property taxes and homeowners insurance with each monthly payment and holds the money until the bills come due. Where is the money held?
choices: With the title company until the next closing
questions.explanation: When the lender collects taxes and insurance along with principal and interest (PITI), it holds them in an escrow or impound account and pays the bills when due.

questions.stem: A lender reviews a borrower's savings to confirm there is enough cash for the down payment, closing costs and reserves. Which of the four Cs of credit is this?
questions.explanation: Capital is the cash for the down payment, closing costs and reserves. Capacity is the ability to afford the payment (income and ratios), credit is payment history, and collateral is the property.

questions.stem: A buyer's broker learns that her client's income is slightly too low to qualify for the loan he wants. What should she do?
choices: Keep the application truthful and refer him to the lender
Suggest he round his income up, since lenders rarely verify it
Advise him to leave a car loan off the application to improve his ratios
Have the seller pay him cash outside closing to show more savings
questions.explanation: Coaching a borrower to misstate income or debts, or hiding payments from the lender, is mortgage fraud. The broker should keep the application truthful and let the lender discuss other loan programs.

questions.stem: A loan's monthly payments are based on a 30-year schedule, but the remaining balance is due in full after 7 years. What is the large final payment called?
questions.explanation: A partially amortized loan doesn't pay itself off, so a lump sum (the balloon) is due at the end. Negative amortization is a growing balance caused by unpaid interest.

questions.stem: On a fully amortized fixed-rate loan, how do the parts of each payment change over the life of the loan?
choices: The interest portion grows and the principal portion shrinks
The total payment rises each year
Payments cover only interest until the final balloon payment
The principal portion grows and the interest portion shrinks
questions.explanation: Equal payments retire the loan by the end of the term. Early payments are mostly interest because the balance is high; as the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal.

questions.stem: A buyer who has never served in the military wants a government-backed loan with no down payment on a home in an eligible rural area. Her income is within the program's limits. Which program is designed for this?
questions.explanation: USDA Rural Development loans serve eligible rural areas, have income limits and often require no down payment. VA loans also may need no down payment, but they are for eligible veterans and service members.

questions.stem: A seller who owns her home free and clear agrees to take part of the price as a note from the buyer, secured by a deed of trust on the home being sold. This is
choices: a home equity line of credit
questions.explanation: When the seller acts as lender and takes back a note secured by the property sold, it is seller financing, often called a purchase-money mortgage. A wraparound requires an existing underlying loan, which this home doesn't have.

questions.stem: A buyer makes monthly payments to the seller on a new, larger loan, and the seller keeps paying her own existing loan out of those payments. What could block this wraparound arrangement?
choices: A cap on the new loan's interest rate
A release clause in the new loan
A due-on-sale clause in the seller's loan
A takeout commitment from a permanent lender
questions.explanation: A wraparound leaves the seller's loan in place after the sale. If that loan has a due-on-sale (alienation) clause, the lender can call it due when the property transfers, which defeats the wrap.

questions.stem: A couple has found their next home but hasn't sold their current one. They need a short-term loan that uses the equity in their current home to buy the new one. Which loan fits?
questions.explanation: A bridge (swing) loan is short-term financing that lets a buyer tap equity in the current home before it sells. A takeout loan replaces a construction loan, and a reverse mortgage pays older owners from their equity.

questions.stem: A buyer's loan on a furnished condo covers both the unit and its furniture and appliances. This is a
questions.explanation: A package loan covers real property plus personal property. A blanket loan covers several parcels, and an open-end loan lets the borrower borrow more later under the same instrument.

questions.stem: A builder pays the lender an up-front amount so that a buyer's interest rate is lower for the first two years of the loan. This is called
choices: a home equity line of credit
questions.explanation: In a buydown, someone (often the seller or builder) pays the lender up front to reduce the borrower's rate, either permanently or for the early years.

questions.stem: A homeowner gets a revolving line of credit secured by her home, usually in second position. She draws as needed and pays interest only on what she uses. This is a
questions.explanation: A HELOC is a revolving line secured by the home. A reverse mortgage instead pays the owner and its balance grows until the owner sells, moves out permanently or dies.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the secondary mortgage market?
choices: To make loans directly to home buyers
To set the index for adjustable-rate loans
To insure lenders against borrower default
To buy existing loans from lenders
questions.explanation: Loans are made in the primary market. The secondary market buys and sells existing loans, which puts money back in lenders' hands so they can lend again. Uniform documents and standards exist largely so loans can be sold there.

questions.stem: A broker accepts a payment from a lender each time she refers a buyer who gets a federally related mortgage loan. Which penalty can apply under RESPA?
choices: A warning letter for a first offense, with no fine
Loss of that sale's commission, but no fine or prison
A fine of up to $10,000, up to one year in prison, or both
A fine equal to the referral fee, with no possibility of prison
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 8 violations can bring a fine of up to $10,000, up to one year in prison, or both, plus civil liability to the borrower for three times the charge paid for the settlement service involved. A lender's per-referral payment to a broker is exactly the kind of kickback Section 8 bans.

questions.stem: A buyer is financing a home with a federally related mortgage loan. As a condition of the sale, the seller insists the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular title company. Under RESPA this is
choices: allowed, because the seller controls the terms of the sale
allowed if the title company gives the seller a discount
allowed if the listing broker discloses it in writing
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 9 bars a seller from requiring, as a condition of sale, that a buyer using a federally related loan buy title insurance from a particular title company; a seller who does so is liable to the buyer for three times the title insurance charges. Neither written disclosure nor a benefit to the seller makes it allowed.

questions.stem: Which federal law requires many lenders to report loan-level data about the applications they receive and the loans they make, so regulators and the public can spot patterns such as redlining?
questions.explanation: HMDA, implemented by Regulation C, is a reporting law. ECOA prohibits credit discrimination, TILA requires cost-of-credit disclosures, and RESPA covers settlement costs and kickbacks.

questions.stem: Under federal ability-to-repay rules, which loan feature generally keeps a loan from being a qualified mortgage?
questions.explanation: Qualified mortgages generally avoid negative amortization, interest-only periods, most balloon payments, terms over 30 years and excessive points and fees. A 15-year fixed-rate loan with documented income fits within the rules.

questions.stem: A lender repeatedly persuades a homeowner to refinance, charging new fees each time without any real benefit to the borrower. This practice is
questions.explanation: Loan flipping is repeated refinancing to generate fees. Packing adds unnecessary products such as credit insurance, and equity stripping is lending against equity without regard to the borrower's ability to pay.

questions.stem: A lender charges higher rates on loans in certain neighborhoods because of the neighborhoods' racial makeup, regardless of the borrowers' credit. This is
questions.explanation: Redlining is refusing to lend, or lending on worse terms, in certain areas because of their racial or ethnic makeup. It is illegal under fair lending laws.

questions.stem: Annual property taxes of $3,240 are paid in arrears and are unpaid at an April 20 closing. Using a 360-day year, with the seller owning the day of closing, how is the proration shown?
choices: $990 credit to the seller and debit to the buyer
$2,250 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
$990 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
$976.44 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: Daily rate: $3,240 ÷ 360 = $9. Seller's days: 3 months × 30 + 20 = 110. Share: 110 × $9 = $990. The buyer will pay the whole bill later, so debit the seller and credit the buyer. $976.44 comes from wrongly using 365 days.

questions.stem: A home is worth $420,000. The owner owes $250,000 on a first deed of trust and $40,000 on a home equity line. What is the owner's equity?
questions.explanation: Equity = market value − all loan balances: $420,000 − $250,000 − $40,000 = $130,000. Forgetting the second loan gives $170,000; $290,000 is the total debt.

questions.stem: An investor pays $250,000 cash for a property that produces $20,000 of annual income. What is the simple rate of return?
questions.explanation: Rate of return = annual income ÷ amount invested: $20,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.08, or 8%. Dividing the other way ($250,000 ÷ $20,000) gives 12.5, which is not a rate of return.

questions.stem: A lot is worth $171,000 after losing 10% of its value. What was it worth originally?
questions.explanation: The current value is 90% of the original: $171,000 ÷ 0.90 = $190,000. Adding 10% of the current value ($171,000 × 1.10 = $188,100) undershoots because the 10% loss was figured on the original value.

questions.stem: An investor buys a property for $750,000, of which $150,000 is land. The building has a 40-year economic life. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the annual depreciation?
questions.explanation: Only the improvement depreciates: $750,000 − $150,000 = $600,000. $600,000 ÷ 40 = $15,000 per year. Dividing the full $750,000 gives $18,750, which wrongly includes the land.

questions.stem: Which expense increases a homeowner's adjusted basis?
questions.explanation: Capital improvements that add value or extend useful life, such as a finished basement, are added to basis. Ordinary repairs and maintenance don't change basis.

questions.stem: A homeowner takes the standard deduction rather than itemizing. Which statement is correct?
choices: She can still deduct her mortgage interest separately
She can deduct her homeowners insurance premiums instead of interest
She can deduct her loan principal payments instead
She gets no separate deduction for mortgage interest or property taxes
questions.explanation: Mortgage interest and property taxes are itemized deductions, so they help only a taxpayer who itemizes. Principal, homeowners insurance and utilities on a personal residence are never deductible.

questions.stem: A couple sells their main home at a $30,000 loss. How is the loss treated for federal income tax purposes?
choices: It is deductible against ordinary income
It is carried over to reduce the gain on their next home
It is not deductible, because it is a personal loss
It is deductible only if they buy another home within two years
questions.explanation: A loss on the sale of your own home is a personal loss and is not deductible. Only gains on a personal residence are taxed, subject to the home-sale exclusion.

questions.stem: An investor buys an office building. Over what period is the building's cost recovered using straight-line depreciation?
choices: It can't be depreciated because it is commercial
questions.explanation: Nonresidential property such as offices, retail and warehouses is recovered over 39 years. Residential rental property uses 27.5 years. Land is never depreciable under either schedule.

questions.stem: How does taking depreciation on a rental property affect the owner when the property is sold?
choices: It lowers basis, which raises the taxable gain
It raises basis, which lowers the taxable gain
It has no effect on basis or gain
It permanently erases tax on that part of the gain
questions.explanation: Each year's depreciation lowers adjusted basis, so the gain on sale is larger. The part of the gain caused by depreciation is taxed under recapture rules, so depreciation defers tax rather than erasing it.

questions.stem: An IRS lien for unpaid federal income tax is best described as
choices: a specific lien on the taxpayer's home only
a lien that always ranks ahead of local property tax liens
a lien that can't reach property acquired after it arises
a general lien on all of the taxpayer's property
questions.explanation: A federal tax lien is a general lien that attaches to all the taxpayer's property, including property acquired later. Local property tax liens are specific liens and, under federal law, can keep priority even over a federal tax lien.

questions.stem: A son inherits his mother's house. She paid $90,000 for it decades ago, and it was worth $480,000 on the date of her death. What is generally his basis?
questions.explanation: An heir's basis in inherited property is generally its fair market value on the date of death, so his basis is $480,000. The mother's $90,000 purchase price does not carry over.

questions.stem: Under FIRPTA, who is generally required to withhold part of the amount realized when the seller is a foreign person?
questions.explanation: FIRPTA puts the withholding duty on the buyer (the transferee), with some exemptions. In practice the closing company usually handles it for the buyer.

questions.stem: A lot seller carries back a loan to a buyer who plans to build. The construction lender requires first lien position before it will fund. What does the seller's loan usually include to allow this?
choices: A lien waiver from each supplier
questions.explanation: With a subordination clause the lot seller agrees that its lien will rank behind the construction loan. A takeout commitment is a permanent lender's promise to pay off the construction loan, and lien waivers come from contractors and suppliers.

questions.stem: Who actually issues licenses and certifications to real property appraisers?
questions.explanation: States license and certify appraisers, using criteria at least as strict as the AQB's minimums. The Appraisal Foundation and its boards set standards and qualifications but license no one, and ARELLO is an association of license regulators.

questions.stem: What is ARELLO?
choices: A private trade association that brokers join for marketing and networking
The federal agency that licenses brokers who work in several states
An association of state and provincial license regulators
The board that writes and interprets appraisal standards
questions.explanation: ARELLO is an association of real estate license regulators. It shares best practices, runs a license verification database and certifies distance-education courses, but it does not license, discipline or write license laws.

questions.stem: An investor's rental building is in excellent condition and rising in value, yet she takes a cost recovery deduction for it every year. Which statement explains this?
choices: She must be claiming external obsolescence
Tax depreciation follows a schedule, not value loss
The land is depreciating even though the building is not
The deduction requires an appraiser to confirm a value loss
questions.explanation: Tax cost recovery is a paper deduction on a fixed schedule whether or not the building loses value. Appraisal depreciation (physical deterioration or functional or external obsolescence) is an actual loss in value. Land never depreciates under either.

questions.stem: A buyer pays $400,000 for a home that appraises at $380,000 and borrows $323,000 on a conventional loan. What is the loan-to-value ratio, and will the lender typically require PMI?
choices: 80.75%; yes, because the LTV is above 80%
85%; no, because PMI applies only to FHA loans
80.75%; no, because the down payment is more than 15%
85%; yes, because the LTV is above 80%
questions.explanation: LTV uses the lesser of price or appraised value: $323,000 ÷ $380,000 = 85%. Conventional loans above 80% LTV typically require PMI, which protects the lender. Dividing by the $400,000 price gives the tempting 80.75%.

questions.stem: A buyer pays $300,000 for a home with a $280,000 loan, and the lender charges 1.5 discount points. How much are the points, and how do they affect the APR?
choices: $4,200; they make the APR lower than the note rate
$4,500; they make the APR higher than the note rate
$4,200; they make the APR higher than the note rate
$420; they have no effect on the APR
questions.explanation: Points are based on the loan: $280,000 × 0.015 = $4,200. The APR includes certain finance charges such as points as well as interest, so it ends up higher than the note rate. Using the $300,000 price gives $4,500.

questions.stem: An office building's NOI is $90,000, and recent sales support a 7.5% capitalization rate. If investors begin demanding a 9% cap rate for similar buildings, what happens to the building's value?
choices: It stays the same because NOI hasn't changed
questions.explanation: At 7.5%: $90,000 ÷ 0.075 = $1,200,000. At 9%: $90,000 ÷ 0.09 = $1,000,000. A higher cap rate means a lower value for the same NOI, so value falls by $200,000.
